# Discussion and Conclusion

## Discussion

This thesis developed, validated, and applied the
hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio as a structural brain aging
biomarker. Across four studies, the work followed a
progression from quality control infrastructure, through
automated biomarker computation and population-level
characterization, to clinical hypothesis testing, producing
a pipeline that transforms a raw MRI scan into an
individualized, age- and sex-referenced brain aging metric.

### From quality control to clinical inference: a cohesive pipeline

Reliable neuroimaging inference requires a complete
methodological chain, starting well before any biomarker is
computed. Qrater (Chapter 3) was developed to address a
practical bottleneck: biobank-scale datasets generate tens
of thousands of images requiring quality assessment at
multiple processing stages, yet existing tools were too
narrowly specialized, lacked collaborative features, or
could not scale to multi-step, multi-rater workflows.
Qrater addressed this gap with a web-based
platform for centralized visual quality control that
accelerated inspection throughput by 2- to 30-fold compared
to conventional methods. Qrater was not an isolated
software contribution but the entry point for the empirical
work that followed: the curated ADNI imaging data produced
through Qrater's deployment served as the foundation for
the HVR validation in Chapter 4 and the clinical analyses
in Chapter 6.

The importance of this foundation is clear when considering
what happens without it. Motion artifacts, registration
failures, and segmentation errors introduce systematic bias
into volumetric measurements, and these biases
disproportionately affect clinical populations, the groups
where accurate measurement matters most
[@reuter_head_2015; @alexander2016subtle]. Chapter 3 showed
that even experts with decades of experience are
inconsistent in quality judgments, not only for borderline
cases but even for images previously deemed obvious
failures, highlighting the need for structured training
protocols and collaborative verification rather than
reliance on individual assessors. This is consistent with
the broader QC literature showing that automated tools,
while useful for triage, cannot replace visual inspection
for subcortical segmentation failures that correlate with
clinical status
[@monereo2021quality; @raamana2023visualqc].

Chapter 4 then established the automated computation that
made population-scale analysis feasible. The convolutional
neural network segmentation achieved a Dice coefficient of
0.94 for hippocampal delineation and maintained high
performance across diagnostic groups, including the
ventricular compartment where traditional atlas-based
methods showed sharp performance drops. The pipeline was
packaged as a publicly available Docker tool, so that any
research group can compute the HVR from a T1-weighted scan
with a single command, using the same segmentation
algorithm employed throughout this thesis. The continuity
from quality-controlled input data (Chapter 3) through
validated automated segmentation (Chapter 4) to normative
referencing (Chapters 5 and 6) means that each link in the
chain has been independently evaluated, an increasingly
important requirement for clinical translation
[@bethlehem_brain_2022; @ge_normative_2024].

### The HVR as a self-normalizing biomarker

The HVR rests on a simple idea: because both hippocampal
volume and adjacent ventricular volume scale with
intracranial volume, their ratio cancels the shared
head-size variance, producing a measure of medial temporal
lobe integrity that is largely independent of the head-size
confound that has long complicated hippocampal volumetry
[@schoemaker2019; @obrien_statistical_2011]. This thesis
provides the first large-scale empirical confirmation of
this self-normalizing property and extends it in two
directions.

First, the UK Biobank analyses in Chapter 5 showed that
the HVR has a much weaker correlation with intracranial
volume than unadjusted hippocampal volume, confirming that
the ratio largely removes the head-size dependence that
drives methodological artifacts in conventional volumetry.
This matters because it directly resolves the
contradictions that have characterized the sex-differences
literature, where the same hippocampal data yield opposite
conclusions depending on the correction method applied
[@pintzka_marked_2015; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020;
@wang_comparison_2024]. The HVR produces directionally
consistent sex-difference estimates regardless of whether
additional intracranial volume adjustments are applied,
providing the stability that a clinically useful biomarker
requires.

Second, the clinical validation in Chapters 4 and 6
showed that the HVR outperforms hippocampal volume alone.
In Chapter 4, the HVR yielded larger effect sizes for
distinguishing cognitively healthy individuals from those
with Alzheimer's disease across all segmentation methods,
and stronger associations with age across most methods.
The improvement was most pronounced for lower-quality
segmentation approaches, suggesting that the ratio partly
compensates for measurement noise because errors in
adjacent tissue and fluid compartments are correlated. In
Chapter 6, sex-specific normative curves derived from the
UK Biobank were applied to the ADNI clinical cohort for
individualized z-scoring along the Alzheimer's disease
continuum. The transfer revealed a systematic negative
z-score offset in ADNI relative to the UK Biobank
reference, reflecting age-distribution and population-health
differences between the two cohorts. Absolute z-scores
therefore require cautious interpretation across datasets,
but within-cohort relative comparisons remained valid. This
cross-dataset transfer represents a step toward the
normative referencing framework envisioned by the brain
charting movement
[@bethlehem_brain_2022; @ge_normative_2024].

The residual negative correlation between the HVR and
intracranial volume, while small, deserves comment. Under
strict isometric scaling, the ratio would be entirely
ICV-independent. The remaining dependence likely reflects
the hyperallometric scaling of the lateral
ventricles (ventricles expand disproportionately in larger
brains), which introduces a mild downward bias in the HVR
for individuals with larger heads
[@de_jong_allometric_2017; @williams_neuroanatomical_2021].
This departure from perfect cancellation is modest compared
to the biases of standard correction methods, but it means
that the HVR is substantially rather than perfectly
self-normalizing. Residualization of the HVR on intracranial
volume remains an option for applications demanding complete
ICV independence, though the incremental gain is small.

### Methodological artifacts masquerading as biology

A recurrent theme across this thesis is that analytical
choices can manufacture apparent biological effects or
obscure genuine ones. Two findings illustrate this clearly.

In Chapter 5, applying different head-size correction
methods to the same UK Biobank dataset produced hippocampal
sex differences that reversed direction, with effect sizes
shifting by approximately 1.5 standard deviations from a
large male advantage (unadjusted volumes) to a moderate
female advantage (proportional correction). The reversal is
explained by the hypoallometric scaling of the hippocampus
relative to intracranial volume: proportional division
over-corrects smaller brains and under-corrects larger ones,
creating a spurious female advantage
[@pintzka_marked_2015; @sanchis-segura_effects_2020]. When
intracranial volume is properly controlled through
residualization or matching, hippocampal volume differences
between the sexes collapse to near-zero
[@nordenskjold_intracranial_2015; @voevodskaya_effects_2014;
@wang_comparison_2024].

In Chapter 6, an analogous artifact appeared in the
cardiovascular risk domain. The Framingham Risk Score
predicted hippocampal decline in all six parallel-process
latent growth curve models. But when the age component
embedded in the score was removed through MIMIC-based
adjustment, the apparent cardiovascular effect on
hippocampal atrophy vanished: the age-adjusted
cardiovascular risk factor predicted hippocampal decline in
none of the six models. A complementary analysis in
amyloid-negative, cognitively unimpaired participants
reinforced this conclusion: the pattern reversed, with
age-adjusted cardiovascular risk reaching significance while
the Framingham Risk Score did not, consistent with the
age component of the score co-varying with amyloid
pathology rather than capturing cardiovascular effects per
se. This dissociation shows that the widely reported link
between the Framingham Risk Score and brain atrophy in
elderly cohorts reflects, at least in large part, the
confound of age-weighting within the score rather than
cerebrovascular pathophysiology
[@koller_development_2012; @pencina_quantifying_2019].

The common lesson is that composite metrics embedding
demographic confounds, whether head size in a proportional
correction or age in a risk score, can generate
associations that appear biologically meaningful but are
artifacts of the metric's construction. This thesis
contributes both the diagnosis of these artifacts and
solutions: the HVR as an alternative to externally
corrected hippocampal volumes, and the MIMIC framework for
deconfounding composite clinical scores. Both build the
adjustment into the measurement itself rather than applying
it post hoc.

### Sex differences: what remains after deconfounding

Once head-size artifacts are removed, genuine sex
differences in hippocampal structure and aging remain, with
implications for clinical practice.

The matched-pair analysis in Chapter 5 demonstrated that
when males and females are strictly matched on age and
intracranial volume, hippocampal volume differences
collapse to effectively zero, but a small but consistent
female HVR advantage persists. This persistent advantage
is driven primarily by males retaining significantly
larger ventricles even after head-size matching, a pattern
consistent with the well-documented earlier onset and
faster progression of ventricular enlargement in males
[@curra_ventricular_2019; @voevodskaya_effects_2014]. The
HVR captures this ventricular signal because it integrates
both tissue and fluid compartments into a single metric,
detecting a sex difference in brain aging that would be
missed by hippocampal volume alone.

The cross-sectional age-stratified analyses further revealed
that males exhibit approximately 1.7-fold steeper
HVR decline with age compared to females, driven
predominantly by the greater rate of male ventricular
expansion rather than differential hippocampal atrophy per
se. This steeper male trajectory widens the female HVR
advantage at older ages, a finding that has direct
implications for age-specific normative thresholds. The
sex-stratified GAMLSS centile curves established in Chapter
5 formalize this requirement: an HVR value at the 50th
percentile for a male of a given age falls well below the
50th percentile for a female of the same age, meaning that
sex-pooled norms would systematically misclassify healthy
males as abnormal and pathological females as normal.

The brain-cognition models in Chapter 5 revealed further
sex-specificity. Residualized hippocampal volume predicted
general cognition in females but not in males, consistent
with evidence that hippocampal structure predicts
associative memory in women but not men
[@zheng_sex_2017; @jockwitz_differential_2024]. The HVR
showed the opposite pattern: significant associations with
cognition in both sexes but stronger coupling in
males, suggesting that the combined tissue-fluid metric
captures aspects of structural integrity relevant to male
cognitive processing that hippocampal volume alone misses.
In the clinical domain, the parallel-process models in
Chapter 6 showed sex-asymmetric hippocampal-cognitive
coupling along the Alzheimer's disease continuum, though
this asymmetry may partly reflect power differences between
the male and female subsamples rather than a purely
biological divergence. Nonetheless, the overall pattern
supports sex-stratified modeling in neuroimaging research
[@ferretti_sex_2018; @ritchie_sex_2018].

The biological mechanisms behind these sex differences are
likely multifactorial. Cumulative estrogen exposure has
neuroprotective effects on the hippocampus, promoting
neurogenesis, preserving synaptic plasticity, and reducing
neuroinflammation [@jett_endogenous_2022; @bettio2017].
Women with longer reproductive spans show younger brain ages
and better preserved hippocampal structure
[@de_lange_womens_2020; @luders_case_2025]. The menopausal
transition, with its rapid drop in estrogen, may accelerate
structural brain aging and contribute to the higher lifetime
prevalence of Alzheimer's disease in women
[@jett_endogenous_2022; @ferretti_sex_2018]. Conversely,
the earlier and faster ventricular expansion in males may
reflect sex differences in cerebrovascular aging, white
matter integrity, or CSF dynamics that are not yet fully
characterized [@curra_ventricular_2019; @peterson_sex_2024; @lohner_relation_2022; @burmistrov_sex_2024].

### Brain-cognition coupling across the aging continuum

Chapters 5 and 6 together show that the HVR captures
hippocampal-cognitive coupling across both healthy aging and
the Alzheimer's disease continuum, extending its validity
beyond the small, cross-sectional samples in which it was
originally evaluated [@schoemaker2019].

In healthy aging (Chapter 5), the HVR predicted general
cognitive performance comparably to residualized hippocampal
volume despite requiring no external head-size
adjustment, a practical advantage because intracranial
volume estimation itself introduces error
[@obrien_statistical_2011; @sanfilipo_correction_2004]. The
effect sizes were small, as is typical in large, cognitively
healthy samples [@ritchie_sex_2018], but statistically
robust and consistent across both sexes.

In the clinical context (Chapter 6), the parallel-process
latent growth curve models showed that longitudinal HVR
decline reliably predicts concurrent cognitive decline
across the Alzheimer's disease spectrum. This coupling was
significant regardless of how cardiovascular risk was
measured, whether using the original Framingham Risk Score
or the age-adjusted latent cardiovascular risk
factor, indicating that hippocampal-cognitive coupling is
not driven by shared age or vascular influences but reflects
a genuine neurodegenerative pathway. This is consistent with
the broader literature showing that longitudinal hippocampal
decline is among the strongest structural predictors of
cognitive deterioration
[@oschwald_brain_2020; @kramer_longitudinal_2007].

The "moderation without mediation" finding in Chapter 6
adds nuance. Age-adjusted cardiovascular risk did not
mediate the pathway from vascular burden to hippocampal
decline (the indirect pathway was null), yet it moderated
the hippocampal-cognitive relationship. Converging evidence
from the amyloid-negative control analysis strengthened this
interpretation: when amyloid pathology was absent,
age-adjusted cardiovascular risk reached significance while
the Framingham Risk Score did not, consistent with a
cardiovascular reserve effect that is masked by
amyloid-driven hippocampal decline in the primary sample.
This pattern is consistent with the cognitive reserve
framework [@stern_cognitive_2012]: cardiovascular burden may
reduce the brain's capacity to maintain cognitive
performance at a given level of structural integrity,
without directly accelerating the structural atrophy itself.
Rather than a simple chain (vascular damage causes atrophy
causes cognitive decline), vascular and neurodegenerative
processes may operate through partly independent pathways
that converge on cognitive outcomes
[@gorelick_vascular_2011; @iadecola_neurovascular_2019].

### Practical and clinical implications

Together, this thesis produced a complete, open-source
pipeline from raw MRI acquisition to individualized brain
aging assessment, with each component publicly available
and independently validated.

Qrater provides a quality control platform that
is not specific to hippocampal analysis or to any particular
neuroimaging pipeline; it can be configured for visual
inspection of any imaging modality or processing step,
as demonstrated for structural MRI and extensible to other
modalities including PET and CT (Chapter 3). The
Docker-packaged HVR computation tool enables
single-command, fully automated extraction of hippocampal
and ventricular volumes from T1-weighted scans, removing the
need for site-specific segmentation software installation
or manual intervention (Chapter 4). The sex-stratified
GAMLSS normative curves translate raw volumes into
age-referenced z-scores, enabling clinicians and researchers
to quantify individual deviation from healthy aging
expectations (Chapters 5 and 6). Finally, the MIMIC age-adjustment framework provides an
approach for deconfounding composite clinical scores whose
constituent components independently predict the outcome
of interest, extending beyond the Framingham Risk Score to
other instruments where age or similar confounds dominate
the score variance (Chapter 6).

These tools address a gap in the brain charting literature:
while large-scale normative references are increasingly
available [@bethlehem_brain_2022; @ge_normative_2024], the
practical infrastructure for computing the underlying
metrics, assuring their quality, and referencing them
against population norms has lagged behind. The pipeline
developed here, from quality-controlled segmentation to
normative z-scoring, shows how such end-to-end workflows
can be built and validated for specific structural
biomarkers.

## Limitations

Each chapter discusses study-specific limitations. The
following addresses cross-cutting limitations that span
multiple chapters.

### Cross-sectional designs

The HVR validation (Chapter 4) and the UK Biobank
sex-differences study (Chapter 5) are cross-sectional:
age-related patterns are inferred from between-person
comparisons rather than within-person trajectories.
Cross-sectional age effects may conflate genuine aging
with cohort effects (differences between birth decades
reflecting historical variation in nutrition, education, or
medical care). The longitudinal analyses in Chapter 6
partially address this by modeling within-person change, but
are restricted to the ADNI clinical population. The UK
Biobank repeat imaging subsample (~10,000 participants with
two or more sessions) will eventually allow within-person
validation of the cross-sectional HVR aging patterns from
Chapter 5.

### Cohort representativeness

Both the UK Biobank and ADNI have well-documented selection
biases. The UK Biobank draws from a volunteer cohort that is
healthier, more educated, and less ethnically diverse than
the general UK population, so the normative curves from
Chapter 5 may not represent the full spectrum of healthy
brain aging [@ritchie_sex_2018]. ADNI enrolls a
predominantly white, highly educated sample enriched for
Alzheimer's disease pathology, and participants who remain
in follow-up are those healthy enough to continue attending
visits, introducing attrition bias that may cause the
Chapter 6 models to underestimate true rates of decline.
Together, these selection effects mean the thesis lacks
validation in community-based, ethnically diverse, or
socioeconomically representative populations.

### The HVR as a composite measure

The HVR conflates hippocampal and ventricular contributions
into a single metric. A declining HVR could reflect
hippocampal shrinkage, ventricular expansion, or both.
In cross-sectional analyses, these cannot be separated.
Chapter 5 examined hippocampal volume, ventricular volume,
and the HVR separately to characterize each component, but
the HVR itself remains an aggregate index. Longitudinal
decomposition, tracking individual rates of hippocampal
atrophy and ventricular expansion within the same
individuals over time, would be needed to determine which
component drives HVR change at different disease stages.

### Normative model transfer

Transferring the UK Biobank-derived GAMLSS normative curves
to the ADNI cohort in Chapter 6 revealed a systematic
negative z-score offset in the ADNI reference group,
reflecting the mismatch between a population-based sample
(ages 45--82) and a clinical cohort with a different age
range and health profile. Within-cohort relative comparisons
remain valid, but absolute z-scores are not directly
interchangeable across datasets without recalibration.
This limitation is inherent to all normative referencing
approaches and highlights the need for multi-cohort norm
construction or site-specific recalibration before
individual-level clinical decisions can be supported
[@ge_normative_2024].

### Cognitive measurement

The cognitive assessments differ between the two datasets.
The UK Biobank battery (Chapter 5) is brief and
population-optimized, lacking a reliable episodic memory
measure, a notable gap given the hippocampus's central role
in memory. The bifactor model's memory-specific factor
failed to achieve stable estimation, limiting evaluation of
hippocampal-memory associations in the healthy aging sample.
ADNI (Chapter 6) provides richer neuropsychological
assessment but uses cohort-specific composite scores not
directly comparable to the UK Biobank measures. No unified
cognitive framework spans both datasets, preventing direct
comparison of brain-cognition coupling across the healthy
and clinical populations examined here.

## Future Directions

### Longitudinal HVR validation

The UK Biobank repeat imaging subsample (~10,000
participants with two or more MRI sessions) provides an
opportunity to validate the cross-sectional HVR aging
patterns from Chapter 5 using within-person longitudinal
data. Individual HVR trajectories can test whether the
sex-differential aging rates observed cross-sectionally
replicate in longitudinal change, and whether baseline HVR
or its rate of decline predicts incident cognitive
impairment or dementia. Longitudinal decomposition of the
HVR into hippocampal and ventricular components would
clarify which compartment drives HVR change at different
life stages and in response to different risk factors.

### Clinical translation and diagnostic thresholds

The GAMLSS normative curves and Docker computation tool
developed in this thesis together enable individual-level
HVR z-scoring from a single T1-weighted scan. However,
the clinical utility of this capability depends on
establishing actionable thresholds. Future work should
determine which HVR z-score cutoffs optimally identify
individuals with accelerated brain aging, predict conversion
from mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's dementia, or
stratify participants for clinical trial enrollment. Such
thresholds would require validation against longitudinal
cognitive outcomes and, ideally, against biomarker-confirmed
Alzheimer's disease pathology (amyloid and tau PET) to
establish the HVR's place within the AT(N) diagnostic
framework [@jack2018].

### Gene-sex interactions

APOE genotype was unavailable in the UK Biobank analyses
(Chapter 5). Given the known interaction between APOE-e4
carrier status and sex in Alzheimer's disease risk (female
APOE-e4 carriers show faster hippocampal atrophy and
greater tau deposition than male carriers
[@park_sex-specific_2025; @buckley_sex_2019;
@ferretti_sex_2018]), testing whether APOE modifies HVR sex
differences and aging trajectories is a priority. The ADNI
cohort provides APOE genotyping for all participants, and
extending the latent growth curve models from Chapter 6 with
APOE-by-sex interaction terms would directly address this
question.

### Extension beyond the hippocampus

The ratiometric and MIMIC frameworks developed in this
thesis are not specific to the hippocampus. The
self-normalizing ratio approach could in principle be
applied to other structure-CSF pairs where tissue loss is
accompanied by adjacent fluid expansion (for example,
caudate-to-frontal-horn ratios or cortical
thickness-to-sulcal width indices). Such extensions would
test whether the advantages of ratiometric measurement
generalize beyond the medial temporal lobe. Similarly, the MIMIC age-adjustment framework is
applicable to other composite clinical scores whose
constituent components independently predict the outcome,
including other cardiovascular risk calculators, frailty
indices, or comorbidity scores commonly used in aging
research.

### Inclusive and diverse validation

The normative curves in this thesis are derived from
predominantly white, educated, volunteer samples.
Replication in non-WEIRD (Western, Educated,
Industrialized, Rich, and Democratic) populations and
community-based cohorts is essential for clinical
generalizability. Extending the HVR normative framework to
ethnically diverse and socioeconomically representative
populations would determine whether the aging trajectories
and sex differences observed here generalize beyond the
cohorts studied.

## Conclusion

This thesis developed, validated, and applied the
hippocampal-to-ventricle ratio as a self-normalizing
structural brain aging biomarker, spanning the full
pipeline from data quality assurance to clinical hypothesis
testing. Each study built upon the preceding work. Quality
control infrastructure was established through Qrater, an
open-source platform that enabled multi-rater curation of
the neuroimaging data underlying all subsequent analyses
(Chapter 3). Automated HVR computation was developed and
validated against manual segmentation, showing superior
effect sizes for Alzheimer's disease group discrimination
and stronger associations with age compared to conventional
hippocampal volumetry (Chapter 4). The HVR's
self-normalizing properties were confirmed in 27,680 UK
Biobank participants, resolving contradictory findings on
hippocampal sex differences by showing that these
discrepancies are methodological artifacts of head-size
correction, and sex-specific normative aging curves were
established for individual-level referencing (Chapter 5).
Finally, the normative framework was transferred to a
clinical Alzheimer's disease cohort, revealing that the
widely reported association between cardiovascular risk and
brain atrophy is largely driven by age-confounding within
the Framingham Risk Score --- a conclusion reinforced by a
complementary analysis in amyloid-negative participants
showing the reversed pattern --- while hippocampal-cognitive
coupling persists regardless of how cardiovascular risk is
measured (Chapter 6).

The scientific contribution of this work is twofold. First,
the HVR succeeds as a self-normalizing biomarker not because
ratios are generically superior (Chapter 5 shows that the
proportions method, itself a ratio-based correction,
produces biologically implausible results when brain
structures scale non-isometrically with head size) but
because the HVR captures a specific anatomical
relationship: the ex-vacuo dilation that accompanies hippocampal
atrophy: as the hippocampus shrinks, the adjacent ventricle
expands to fill the vacated space, so the ratio captures
both changes. It is this anatomical relationship, not
the arithmetic of division, that makes the HVR resistant
to head-size confounding where
other correction strategies fail. Second, methodological
vigilance in quality control, head-size adjustment, and
risk score construction is not peripheral to scientific
discovery but is itself how artifacts are distinguished from
biology. The reversal of hippocampal sex differences across
correction methods and the disappearance of cardiovascular
risk effects upon age adjustment --- confirmed by the
complementary reversal in amyloid-negative participants ---
are not secondary findings; they show that the field's prior
conclusions on these topics were, in part, products of
analytical tools rather than of the underlying
neurobiology.

The HVR pipeline developed here, from quality-controlled
segmentation to sex-stratified normative z-scoring, is
publicly available, fully automated, and validated across
two major neuroimaging cohorts. It provides a reproducible framework for structural brain aging research,
and a foundation for future longitudinal validation,
clinical threshold development, and extension to diverse
populations.
